idiom_name: class PersonRow { static std::optional<PersonRow> find(...); void insert(...); void update(...); } over sqlite3
implementation_notes: One class per table, fields mirroring the columns, a static find(sqlite3*, key) returning std::optional<Row>, and insert/update/delete members taking the connection. Wrap sqlite3_stmt in a small RAII type (unique_ptr with a finalize deleter, or a three-line wrapper class) so every error path releases the statement; bind parameters with sqlite3_bind_* and read columns with sqlite3_column_*. This is the pattern exactly as written - no dependency, explicit SQL, and the gateway stays a plain data holder.
pitfalls: A raw sqlite3* member outliving the connection is a use-after-free; the connection should be passed per call, not stored in the row.
Wrapping sqlite3_stmt with a custom deleter is the difference between exception safety and a leak on every thrown bind error.
Returning std::string built from sqlite3_column_text is mandatory - the pointer dies with the next step.

variants.name: sqlite_orm storage CRUD over a plain row struct
variants.implementation_notes: The row stays a plain aggregate (or a struct with make_table/column_pointer mapping) and the storage object plays the finder and gateway roles: storage.get<Person>(id) for the find, storage.insert / storage.update / storage.remove for the writes. This removes the hand-written statements at the price of a heavy template header and compile-time errors that name template internals; choose it when the schema is simple and the team prefers declarative mapping to explicit SQL.
variants.idiom_name: sqlite_orm::make_storage(...) with storage.get/insert/update/remove on an aggregate struct
pitfalls: Template error messages for a mis-declared column are enormous; keep the mapping in one translation unit.
The storage must outlive every row operation and is not thread-safe without external serialisation.
